legal.headline: Law student moves Kerala High Court against restrictions under new internship policy
legal.hook: Law student moves Kerala High Court against restrictions under new internship policy
legal.summary: The Court granted interim relief to the student while leaving open the larger question concerning the validity and applicability of the restrictions imposed under the High Court's internship policy.
legal.contextNote: The Kerala High Court's interim order tests judicial administrative discretion against fundamental rights under Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution of India. While the Bar Council of India Rules on Legal Education govern mandatory student internships under the Advocates Act, 1961, individual High Courts exercise administrative autonomy in framing clerkship and internship schemes. No direct Supreme Court precedent addresses restrictive judicial internship eligibility, though administrative arbitrariness principles under State of Bihar v. Upendra Narayan Singh (2009) apply. (1) Corporate legal departments and law firms running structured student placement programs should audit their eligibility criteria to ensure non-discriminatory classification that withstands constitutional scrutiny. (2) Practice managers relying on judicial clerks or interns for court liaison must review short-term staffing models, as any final ruling invalidating administrative restrictions will broaden the applicant pool for High Court clerkships nationwide.

legal.contextNote: Governance battles over Tata Sons directly intersect with the Maharashtra Public Trusts Act, 1950 (MPT Act) and the jurisdiction of the Joint Charity Commissioner. Under Sections 41A (power to issue directions) and 41E (injunctions), factional trustee disputes convert trust law remedies into leverage over corporate voting rights in holding entities, testing the principles outlined in Tata Consultancy Services Ltd. v. legal.headline: Cabinet approves 3% hike in Dearness Allowance and Dearness Relief from 1 July 2026
legal.hook: Union Cabinet has approved a 3% DA and DR hike, increasing the rate from 60% to 63% with effect from 1 July 2026
legal.summary: Union Cabinet has approved a 3% DA and DR hike, increasing the rate from 60% to 63% with effect from 1 July 2026 Cabinet approves a 3% increase in Dearness Allowance and Dearness Relief, raising the rate from 60% to 63% from 1 July 2026. On 28 October 2026, the Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Mr. Narendra Modi, approved the release of an additional instalment of Dearness Allowance (DA) to Central Government employees and Dearness Relief (DR) to Central Government pensioners, enhancing the rate by 3% from 60% to 63% of Basic Pay/Pension.
legal.contextNote: Executive DA revisions stem from Article 309 of the Constitution and the Central Civil Services (Revised Pay) Rules, 2016. While routine fiscal updates face no direct constitutional challenge, the Supreme Court in Deokinandan Prasad v. State of Bihar (1971) affirmed that accrued retirement benefits and allowances constitute protected property under Article 300A. For corporate in-house counsel: (1) Audit joint venture entities, defense contractors, and private payrolls pegged to central DA rates to recalculate wage liabilities and accrue retroactive arrears from July 2026. (2) Re-calculate statutory employer contributions under Section 2(b) of the Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, and Section 2(s) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, as elevated DA directly expands mandatory statutory benefit baselines. (3) Review government procurement and service contracts featuring labor price variation clauses to submit formal escalation claims for expanded labor overheads.

(2) Law firms and corporate legal departments setting up junior counsel retainer structures should benchmark their stipends against this ₹30,000 monthly threshold to attract top-tier appellate talent. legal.headline: Can staying on at a protest beyond permitted hours attract Section 223(a) BNS? Delhi HC quashes FIR
legal.hook: The Court held that mere presence at a demonstration does not establish offences under Sections 223(a) and 3(5) BNS, i.e.
legal.summary: The Court held that mere presence at a demonstration does not establish offences under Sections 223(a) and 3(5) BNS, i.e. disobedience of a duly promulgated order by public servant
legal.contextNote: Section 223(a) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 replaces Section 188 IPC regarding disobedience to public orders. The Delhi High Court aligns with established constitutional jurisprudence in *Madhu Limaye v. SDM Monghyr* (1970), reinforcing that passive presence at a demonstration lacks criminal *mens rea* and cannot trigger prosecution without proof of conscious defiance. Crucially, Section 223 BNS offences remain procedurally restricted under Section 215 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 (formerly Section 195 CrPC), which bars courts from taking cognizance without a formal written complaint by the public servant concerned. (1) In-house and criminal litigation counsel should invoke this ruling alongside Section 528 BNSS (quashing powers) to discharge corporate officers or field personnel swept into blanket FIRs during site-level agitations or industrial disputes. (2) Update corporate crisis handling SOPs to ensure local management cleanly separates peaceful presence from unlawful assembly, preventing vicarious liability claims under Section 3(5) BNS.
